q: Why do airplane windows have rounded corners?
a: Square corners concentrate stress and start cracks
w: Rounded glass is cheaper to make
They give passengers a wider view
x: The de Havilland Comet crashes of 1954 taught the industry how fast metal fatigue cracks grow from sharp corners.

q: At what frequency does household power alternate in the United States?
x: Most of Europe, Asia and Africa use 50 Hz. Japan uses both, split down the middle of the country.

q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
x: Gallium is the trap: it melts at about 30 °C, so it turns liquid in your hand, but not on a table.

q: Why are most manhole covers round?
a: A circle can't fall through its own opening
w: Round covers are cheaper to cast
Round holes are faster to dig
x: A square cover can slip through diagonally. A round one is the same width in every direction.

q: What type of bridge is the Golden Gate Bridge?
x: The deck hangs from two main cables draped over the towers. In a cable-stayed bridge, the cables run straight from the towers to the deck.

q: Which gas was usually sealed inside old-fashioned incandescent light bulbs?
x: An inert gas slows the tungsten filament from evaporating. Oxygen would burn it out almost instantly.

q: What color is an airplane's “black box” flight recorder?
x: Orange makes it easier to find in wreckage. The name probably comes from early recorders' dark casings.

q: The unit of power, the watt, is named after which inventor?
x: Watt's steam engine improvements drove the Industrial Revolution. He also coined “horsepower” to sell his engines.

q: What is the minimum number of satellites a GPS receiver needs to find its position in 3D?
x: Three would be enough if your phone had a perfect clock. The fourth satellite solves for the clock error.

q: The Eiffel Tower was originally built as…
a: a temporary entrance arch for a World's Fair
w: a monument to the French Revolution
an observation tower for the French army
x: It was built for the 1889 Exposition with a 20-year permit. Being useful as a radio antenna helped save it.

q: Why does the Leaning Tower of Pisa lean?
a: Soft ground under one side of its foundation
w: Bombing damage in World War II
x: It started tilting during construction in the 1170s, when the first floors sank into soft clay.

q: What is the main ingredient in ordinary window glass?
x: Silica sand is melted with soda ash and lime, which lower its melting point.

q: Which country holds the speed record for a train running on regular wheels and rails?
x: A French TGV hit 574.8 km/h in 2007. Japan's record of 603 km/h is for a maglev, which floats instead of using wheels.

q: Roughly how fast does sound travel through air at sea level?
x: That's about 343 meters per second, which is where the 343 trap comes from.

q: Which element makes stainless steel “stainless”?
x: At least 10.5% chromium forms a thin oxide layer that heals itself when scratched.

q: QR codes were invented in Japan in 1994 to track what?
x: Denso Wave, a Toyota supplier, needed something faster to scan than barcodes on the assembly line.

q: Who is often called the first computer programmer?
x: In 1843 she published an algorithm for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a machine that was never finished.

q: Why are car tires black?
a: Carbon black is added to make them stronger
w: Black rubber grips the road better when hot
x: Natural rubber is milky white. Carbon black adds strength and blocks UV light, which makes tires last far longer.

q: What is the most common element in Earth's crust?
x: Oxygen is about 46% of the crust by mass, locked up in rocks as silicates and oxides. Silicon is second.

q: What does “Wi-Fi” stand for?
x: A branding firm coined it in 1999 to sound like Hi-Fi. “Wireless Fidelity” was attached afterward.

q: What inspired the invention of Velcro?
a: Burrs stuck to a dog's fur
x: George de Mestral looked at burdock burrs under a microscope after a walk in 1941 and saw tiny hooks.

q: How does the Panama Canal get ships across Panama?
a: Locks lift them up to a lake above sea level
w: Ships are carried on rail cars
x: Ships rise about 26 meters to Gatun Lake and are lowered again on the other side.

q: Which of these was invented first?
x: Alexander Bain patented a fax machine in 1843, more than 30 years before the telephone in 1876.

q: Why do bridges have gaps called expansion joints?
a: The bridge grows and shrinks with temperature
x: A long steel bridge can change length by more than a meter between winter and summer.

q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
x: It's about 8 minutes and 20 seconds, so the Sun you see is how it looked 8 minutes ago.

q: In which decade was the first email sent?
x: Ray Tomlinson sent it in 1971 on ARPANET, and picked the @ sign to separate the user from the computer.

q: The microwave oven was invented after an engineer working on what noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket?
x: Percy Spencer was working on radar magnetrons at Raytheon in 1945.

q: Why is the Statue of Liberty green?
w: Green glass was mixed into the metal
x: It arrived copper-brown in 1886 and turned green within about 30 years. The patina now protects the metal underneath.

q: Concrete hardens because it…
x: This reaction is called hydration. Concrete even sets underwater, and it keeps getting stronger for years.

q: Why do golf balls have dimples?
a: They reduce drag so the ball flies farther
w: They make the ball easier to grip
They're left over from the molding process
They make the ball spin less
x: The dimples make the air around the ball turbulent, which keeps it hugging the ball and shrinks the drag-causing wake behind it.
